questions.q: At what point does Terraform's job for a newly-provisioned SQL Server resource end, per this lesson?
options: Once the resource itself exists — Terraform doesn't know or care about logins, databases, or jobs inside the instance
Terraform's job never ends; it continuously manages logins and databases too
Terraform's job ends before the resource is even created
Terraform manages everything, including restoring databases and creating logins
questions.explain: The lesson draws the line precisely at resource existence — everything SQL-Server-internal is out of Terraform's scope.

questions.q: What is a Terraform `output` block used for in this pipeline?
options: Exposing a value, like the server's FQDN, after apply so a downstream script can use it
Deleting the resource after it's created
Running a PowerShell script directly from within Terraform
Storing SQL login passwords in plain text permanently
questions.explain: The output value is how the pipeline passes the newly-provisioned server's connection details to the next step.

questions.q: Which tasks does this lesson assign to the post-provisioning PowerShell/dbatools script rather than Terraform?
options: Creating specific logins, restoring an initial database, and setting up SQL Agent jobs
Creating the resource group and virtual network
Choosing the Azure region for the deployment
Setting the VM's compute size
questions.explain: These SQL-Server-internal tasks don't map cleanly to Terraform's resource lifecycle model, so a dbatools script handles them instead.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say forcing a database restore into a Terraform resource usually produces a worse result?
options: Terraform's resource model is built around create/update/destroy lifecycle semantics that a restored database doesn't naturally fit
Terraform cannot execute any script of any kind under any circumstances
Database restores are illegal to automate under Microsoft licensing
dbatools cannot be called from a pipeline
questions.explain: The mismatch is architectural — Terraform's resource lifecycle model isn't a natural fit for an action like a database restore.

questions.q: In the real pipeline order this lesson describes, what happens immediately after `terraform apply` provisions the resource?
options: The pipeline captures the resource's connection details from Terraform's output, before the PowerShell/dbatools script runs
The server is immediately destroyed and re-provisioned
A DSC configuration runs before Terraform even starts
Nothing — the pipeline ends at that point
questions.explain: Capturing Terraform's output is the step that bridges provisioning to the PowerShell/dbatools configuration step that follows.
